notes.heading: Gauss — Arithmetic sequences and series
notes.body:
An arithmetic sequence is an ordered list of numbers that increase by the same fixed amount, called the common difference.
The common difference can be negative: {13, 7, 1, −5, …} has d = −6, so the “increase” is negative.
With first term a and common difference d: tₙ = a + (n − 1)d.
The sum of the first n terms is Sₙ = n/2 × (2a + (n − 1)d).
Example 1: {1, 4, 7, 10, …}; a = 1, d = 3; t₁₀₀ = 1 + 99 × 3 = 298.
Example 2: t₈ = 50 and t₂₀ = 14. Subtracting a + 7d = 50 and a + 19d = 14 gives 12d = −36, d = −3, a = 71.
Example 3: {13, 7, 1, −5, …}; S₄₉ = 49/2 × (2 × 13 + 48 × (−6)) = −6419.
notes.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf pp.1–2

notes.heading: Gauss — Geometric sequences
notes.body:
A sequence is geometric if tₙ₊₁ = r tₙ for a fixed common ratio r. With first term a, tₙ = arⁿ⁻¹.
Example 4: {768, 384, 192, …}; r = 1/2; t₁₅ = 768 × (1/2)¹⁴ = 3/64.
Example 5: t₂₀ = 24 and t₂₃ = 648. Dividing gives r³ = 27, so r = 3.
Example 6: {…, 5, x, 245, …}; 5r² = 245, so r = 7 or −7 and x = 35 or −35.
notes.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf pp.3–4

notes.heading: Gauss — Prime decomposition and counting factors
notes.body:
Every integer greater than 1 is either a prime or a product of two or more primes; the prime decomposition is unique apart from order.
For distinct primes p, q, …, r: d(pᵃqᵇ…rᶜ) = (a + 1)(b + 1)…(c + 1).
360 = 2³ × 3² × 5, so d(360) = 4 × 3 × 2 = 24.
Example 1: 32 = 2⁵, giving 6 factors. 75 = 3 × 5², giving 2 × 3 = 6 factors.
Example 2: Find all two-digit numbers with exactly 12 factors.
For distinct primes p, q and r, the cases are:
Factorisation of 12 | Form of n | Two-digit answers
12 | p¹¹ | Smallest is 2¹¹ = 2048, too big.
2 × 6 | p¹q⁵ | 3¹ × 2⁵ = 96
3 × 4 | p²q³ | 3² × 2³ = 72
2 × 2 × 3 | p¹q¹r² | 3 × 5 × 2² = 60; 3 × 7 × 2² = 84; 2 × 5 × 3² = 90
Thus the numbers are 60, 72, 84, 90 and 96.
notes.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf pp.19–21

notes.heading: Gauss — Expanding and factorising
notes.body:
The distributive law pairs each term in one bracket with each term in the other: (a + b)(c + d) = ac + ad + bc + bd.
Example 1: (x + y)² = (x + y)(x + y) = x² + xy + yx + y² = x² + 2xy + y².
Example 2: (3x + y − 3)(−2x + y + 1) = −6x² + y² + xy + 9x − 2y − 3.
notes.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf pp.34–35

notes.heading: Gauss — Pythagoras’ theorem
notes.body:
For triangle ABC with opposite sides a, b and c: a² + b² = c² if and only if angle C is a right angle.
The longest side of a right-angled triangle is called the hypotenuse.
Example 2: Sides 5, 12 and 13. Since 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13², the angle opposite the side of length 13 is a right angle. The largest angle is 90°.
For sides a, b and c opposite angles A, B and C: a² + b² > c² if and only if angle C is acute; a² + b² = c² if and only if angle C is right; a² + b² < c² if and only if angle C is obtuse.
Example 3: Explain why a triangle with sides 6, 7 and 8 must be acute-angled. Since 6² + 7² > 8², 7² + 8² > 6² and 6² + 8² > 7², each angle is acute.
notes.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf pp.69–70

exams.instructions: These questions are Gauss worked examples. The worked solutions also appear in the Notes, so attempt each question before reading them. Marks (2–3 per question) and time are author-assigned for self-practice, not an exam prediction.

questions.prompt: Gauss p.1, Example 1. Find the 100th term of {1, 4, 7, 10, …}.
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf p.1

questions.prompt: Gauss p.2, Example 2. The 8th term of an arithmetic sequence is 50 and the 20th term is 14. Find the first term.
questions.modelAnswer: 50 = a + 7d and 14 = a + 19d. Subtracting gives 12d = −36, so d = −3. Then a = 50 + 21 = 71.
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf p.2

questions.prompt: Gauss p.2, Example 3. For {13, 7, 1, −5, …}, find the sum of the first 49 terms.
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf p.2

questions.prompt: Gauss p.3, Example 4. Find the 15th term of {768, 384, 192, …}.
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf p.3

questions.prompt: Gauss p.3, Example 5. The 20th and 23rd terms are 24 and 648. Find the common ratio.
questions.modelAnswer: 24 = ar¹⁹ and 648 = ar²². Divide: r³ = 648 ÷ 24 = 27. Therefore r = 3.
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf p.3

questions.prompt: Gauss p.3, Example 6. Find x in the geometric sequence {…, 5, x, 245, …}.
questions.modelAnswer: 5r² = 245, so r² = 49, giving r = 7 or −7. Therefore x = 35 or −35.
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf p.3

questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf p.21

questions.prompt: Gauss p.21, Example 2. Find all two-digit numbers with exactly 12 factors.
questions.modelAnswer:
For distinct primes p, q and r, the cases are:
Factorisation of 12 | Form of n | Two-digit answers
12 | p¹¹ | Smallest is 2¹¹ = 2048, too big.
2 × 6 | p¹q⁵ | 3¹ × 2⁵ = 96
3 × 4 | p²q³ | 3² × 2³ = 72
2 × 2 × 3 | p¹q¹r² | 3 × 5 × 2² = 60; 3 × 7 × 2² = 84; 2 × 5 × 3² = 90
Thus the numbers are 60, 72, 84, 90 and 96.

questions.prompt: Gauss p.35, Example 1. Expand and simplify (x + y)².
questions.modelAnswer: (x + y)(x + y) = x² + xy + yx + y² = x² + 2xy + y².

questions.prompt: Gauss p.35, Example 2. Expand and simplify (3x + y − 3)(−2x + y + 1).
questions.modelAnswer: −6x² + 3xy + 3x − 2xy + y² + y + 6x − 3y − 3 = −6x² + y² + xy + 9x − 2y − 3.

questions.prompt: Gauss p.70, Example 2. What is the largest angle in a triangle with sides 5, 12 and 13?
questions.modelAnswer: 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13². There is a right angle opposite the side of length 13. The largest angle is 90°.
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf p.70

questions.prompt: Gauss p.70, Example 3. Explain why a triangle with sides 6, 7 and 8 must be acute-angled.
questions.modelAnswer: Since 6² + 7² > 8², 7² + 8² > 6² and 6² + 8² > 7², each angle is acute.

questions.prompt: Find all possible values of the first term of a geometric sequence, given t₃ = 500 and t₇ = 312 500.
questions.modelAnswer: r⁴ = t₇ ÷ t₃ = 312 500 ÷ 500 = 625, so r = 5 or r = −5 (since the index is even). For either value, a = t₃ ÷ r² = 500 ÷ 25 = 20. There are two different geometric sequences, with the same first term.
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf pp.4, 89

questions.prompt: The population of a species increases by 5% each year. How many years will it take for the population to be at least double its original size?
questions.modelAnswer: After n years, the population increases by a factor of 1.05ⁿ. We need the least n for which this factor is at least 2. By guess-and-check, 1.05¹⁴ ≈ 1.98 and 1.05¹⁵ ≈ 2.08. So it will take 15 years.
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf pp.4, 89

questions.prompt: How many factors does 5² × 9³ × 13⁴ have?
questions.modelAnswer: 9 is not prime, so write 9³ as (3²)³ = 3⁶. Then d(3⁶ × 5² × 13⁴) = (6 + 1) × (2 + 1) × (4 + 1) = 7 × 3 × 5 = 105.
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf pp.21, 97

questions.prompt: Which number has more factors: 3 million or 4 million?
questions.modelAnswer: 1 000 000 = 10⁶ = (2 × 5)⁶ = 2⁶ × 5⁶. Therefore d(3 000 000) = d(2⁶ × 3¹ × 5⁶) = 7 × 2 × 7 = 98, and d(4 000 000) = d(2⁸ × 5⁶) = 9 × 7 = 63. So 3 million has more factors than 4 million.
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf pp.21, 97

questions.prompt: Find the smallest number with exactly 55 factors.
questions.modelAnswer: A number with 55 factors has the form p⁵⁴ or p⁴q¹⁰. The number 2⁵⁴ has 17 digits. For the other form, letting p = 3 and q = 2 gives 3⁴ × 2¹⁰ = 82 944, which is considerably smaller!
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf pp.21, 97

questions.prompt: An even number has exactly 27 factors, one of which is 117. Find the number.
questions.modelAnswer: The number is even, so 2 is one prime factor. Also, 117 = 9 × 13 = 3² × 13, so 3 and 13 are another two prime factors. A number with 27 factors has the form p²⁶, p²q⁸ or p²q²r². Rule out the first two because there are at least three prime factors. So the number is 2² × 3² × 13² = 6084.
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf pp.21, 97

questions.prompt: Describe all possible right-angled triangles with one side of length 20 and another side of length 21.
questions.modelAnswer: By SSS congruence, specify all three side lengths. If 20 and 21 are the short sides, c² = 20² + 21² = 400 + 441 = 841, so c = √841 = 29. If 21 is the hypotenuse, b² = 21² − 20² = 441 − 400 = 41, so b = √41 (≈ 6.40).
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf pp.71, 122

questions.prompt: A triangle has sides of length 23, 31 and 41. What kinds of angles does it have?
questions.modelAnswer: Since 23² + 31² = 529 + 961 = 1490 < 1681 = 41², the angle opposite the side of length 41 is obtuse, and the other two angles must be acute.
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf pp.71, 122

questions.prompt: An isosceles triangle has base length 6 and area 12. What is its perimeter?
questions.modelAnswer: From A = ½bh, 12 = ½ × 6 × h, so h = 4. Split the isosceles triangle into two congruent right-angled triangles with short sides ½b = 3 and h = 4. By Pythagoras’ theorem each hypotenuse is 5. The perimeter is 6 + 2 × 5 = 16.
questions.source: 2026 Maths Enrichment Gauss Student Notes.pdf pp.71, 122
